title: Rippling Workflow: How to Build One (2026 Guide)
summary: A rippling workflow automates your routine tasks. You'll be able to set up each stage and activate automation for your account.
body_markdown:
## Activepieces for Work That Leaves Rippling


Add[Activepieces](https://www.activepieces.com/) , an automation tool with an MIT-licensed core, only when a Rippling event has to trigger work in an app Rippling can't reach. The task should also repeat often enough that a manual checklist keeps getting missed.


### What it can and can't do with Rippling


Check access first, because most failed builds here are permission failures.


Confirm that your Rippling plan and admin role allow API or webhook access, and whether Activepieces currently lists a Rippling integration; the` packages/pieces/community` folder in its MIT-licensed GitHub monorepo is where that list is counted.


If it doesn't, a webhook trigger fed by Rippling is the fallback.


Don't build until one of those paths is confirmed, or you'll debug a flow that never receives an event.


The catalogue behind that question is countable: the` packages/pieces/community` directory of the MIT-licensed Activepieces monorepo on GitHub holds **750 integrations** , a figure counted from that folder rather than quoted from a marketing page, and roughly 60% of them were contributed by the community, so most of your available integrations come from community maintainers rather than Rippling staff.


If the connector you need isn't among them, you can generate one with AI and add it privately to your own instance, with no vendor release to wait for. MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties run Activepieces in production.


Activepieces reacts to events and calls other apps across those 750 integrations, so the integration layer won't be a bottleneck. It doesn't replace Rippling's approvals, and it doesn't see Rippling data the connecting account can't see.


The flow is only as informed as that account's permissions.


If a field is hidden from the integration, the flow gets an empty value, and an empty value isn't an error. Add a condition that halts the flow when required fields are blank.


The Free plan, at $0 with 1,000 credits a month and unlimited flows, is enough to test that guard against a throwaway record, meaning you validate the concept before any paid usage.


Take a termination, the clearest case. The diagram shows Rippling holding the event and passing it to an Activepieces flow, which fans out to three outside apps, with a bracket marking the steps that never leave Rippling.


A run is 1 credit however many steps it has, so the fan-out and the completion note cost the same as a flow with one step.


Order the work like this:


1. Rippling records the termination and runs its own steps: approvals, final pay and the apps it already deprovisions. These stay native.
2. The event reaches the Activepieces flow, which first checks that the employee ID, end date and manager fields are present.
3. The flow closes the employee's account in a ticketing system, removes them from a team chat workspace and rotates a shared credential in a password vault.
4. The flow posts a completion note to the IT queue, so a failure shows up as a missing note rather than silence.


Everything before step 2 is Rippling's job. Everything after it is the part Rippling can't do.
